clue.text: Nem con? Such a relief!

definitions.meaning: nem con, no one contradicting, is everyone voting aye: read as ALL AYE-ING
soothing or easing a pain or fear is a relief

explanation.surface: A unanimous vote comes as a great relief to the chairman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nem con' (Latin, no one dissenting) describes a vote where all say 'aye', and the answer split as ALL AYING says just that.
explanation.definitionFit: Easing pain or worry gives relief; nem con means a unanimous vote of ayes.

clue.text: Heard by Omar Khayyam when young it was great!

definitions.text: Heard by Omar Khayyam when young it was great!

parts.words: Heard by Omar Khayyam when young it was great!
parts.note: Fitzgerald's Rubaiyat has the poet in youth hear 'great' talk from doctor and saint about it and about

explanation.surface: A remark about what the Persian poet listened to in his youth.
explanation.walkthrough: In Fitzgerald's Rubaiyat: 'Myself when young did eagerly frequent / Doctor and Saint, and heard great argument / About it and about'.
explanation.definitionFit: Heated debate between people, as the poet heard from doctor and saint.

clue.text: Omits the burgeoning

definitions.meaning: trees in spring putting out their foliage

explanation.surface: Someone skips over the spring growth.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase it means omits; read as words it is trees putting out new foliage.
explanation.definitionFit: Excludes or misses out; also, in spring, the foliage coming out on trees.

clue.text: Time for feeding the locust

parts.note: the prophet Joel speaks of restoring what the locust hath eaten, a period of time

explanation.surface: A remark about the hour when insects are fed.
explanation.walkthrough: Joel 2:25: 'I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten'.
explanation.definitionFit: Long periods of time, which the Bible says the locust devoured.

clue.text: Frozen food forbidden, so they say

parts.note: not, as in 'not allowed', expresses something forbidden
ices are frozen desserts

explanation.surface: A rumour that frozen food has been banned.
explanation.walkthrough: Posted announcements are what 'they say': the sign that tells you things.
explanation.definitionFit: Public announcements put up in writing tell people things, as signs do.

clue.text: Discerned about a hundred. How piquant !

indicators.note: the word for discerned goes round, about, the letter for a hundred

parts.note: to discern something is to spy it
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: Someone notices a hundred of something and exclaims at how sharp it is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts C inside SPIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Food with spice in it tastes sharp and piquant.

clue.text: Dadaism? Hardly

parts.note: Dadaism is an art movement, but read as dad-ism it means being a dad

explanation.surface: Doubt whether something counts as the Dada art movement.
explanation.walkthrough: Dadaism was an anti-art movement; split as dad-ism it is the state of being a father, and 'Hardly' says this is not the art.
explanation.definitionFit: Fatherhood, the state of being a dad.

clue.text: The poet's inclination to love

parts.note: a cant is a slope or tilt, an inclination
love is nil in tennis scoring, so O

explanation.surface: A poet leans towards romance.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is short: the poet's division, a section of a long poem.
explanation.definitionFit: A major division of a long poem, such as Dante's, belongs to the poet.

clue.text: Enough! No more!

parts.note: two cries to someone to stop what they are doing

explanation.surface: An exasperated plea for something to stop.
explanation.definitionFit: To cease or stop doing something, which the cries demand.

clue.text: Digs those confounded fairies !

parts.note: D, as in D-, stands for damned, and confounded is a mild form of damned
elves are small fairies

explanation.surface: An angry gardener curses the fairies for digging up the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'D' is the printed abbreviation for a curse such as damned, which 'confounded' softens.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig is to burrow into the ground, as a researcher burrows into a subject.

clue.text: The more reliable the product the less the purchaser needs to rely on it

definitions.text: The more reliable the product the less the purchaser needs to rely on it

parts.words: The more reliable the product the less the purchaser needs to rely on it
parts.note: describes the maker's written promise of repair or refund that comes with goods, needed only if they fail

explanation.surface: A shopper's reflection on good products and after-sales promises.
explanation.definitionFit: A maker's written pledge to repair or replace faulty goods is only called on when the product fails.

clue.text: Shades of being sent back about nothing !

indicators.note: the word sent goes round, about, the letter for nothing
being sent back means the assembled letters are read in the reverse direction

parts.note: O is the round figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone describes shades of being sent back, apparently over nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts O inside SENT to make SENOT, and 'back' turns that round.
explanation.definitionFit: Shades of a colour are its tints or hues, different tones of it.

clue.text: Equestrian encounters

definitions.meaning: hunt gatherings of horses and riders before the chase are called by this name
comes across, or comes face to face with

explanation.surface: Horse riders come across one another.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a hunt's gathering of riders and hounds before setting off is called a meet.
explanation.definitionFit: Fox-hunting gatherings of riders bear the name; as a verb it means comes across someone.

clue.text: Like Alph's measureless background?

parts.note: Coleridge's Kubla Khan has Alph, the sacred river, run through caverns measureless to man

explanation.surface: A question about the setting of the river in Coleridge's poem.
explanation.walkthrough: In Kubla Khan, 'Alph, the sacred river, ran / Through caverns measureless to man': the river's background is hollow and vast.
explanation.definitionFit: Huge hollow spaces underground, like those in the poem, are vast and deep.

clue.text: North with bags of pasta

parts.note: bags of something, like oodles, means a great amount

explanation.surface: Someone from the north with plenty of pasta.
explanation.definitionFit: Long strips of dough are a kind of pasta.

clue.text: Not that this churchman confines himself to lyrics

definitions.text: Not that this churchman confines himself to lyrics

parts.words: Not that this churchman confines himself to lyrics
parts.note: a lay is a song or lyric, but the churchman is a lay person reading services

explanation.surface: A remark that a churchman does not just read poems.
explanation.walkthrough: A lay is a ballad, so this might seem a reader of songs; in fact he is a layman licensed to lead services.
explanation.definitionFit: A layman authorised to read prayers and lead some church services.

clue.text: " Little breezes dusk and" (Tennyson)

parts.note: a gap-fill quotation from The Lady of Shalott, where little breezes darken and tremble the water

explanation.surface: A line from Tennyson with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's The Lady of Shalott has 'Willows whiten, aspens quiver, / Little breezes dusk and shiver'; the missing word rhymes with quiver.
explanation.definitionFit: The breezes tremble the water, quivering as with cold.

clue.text: How the heat might knock one out

definitions.text: How the heat might knock one out

parts.words: How the heat might knock one out
parts.note: a heat is a preliminary round of a race, which puts out the losers

explanation.surface: A remark about being overcome by hot weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heat' suggests hot weather, but it is a qualifying round of a race, which knocks out those who lose.
explanation.definitionFit: To knock out or remove from a competition, as a qualifying round does.

clue.text: Old African beads on a dark lady press heavily!

parts.note: aggri (or aggry) beads are old glass beads from West Africa
Eve is a lady's name, and eve is evening, when it gets dark

explanation.surface: Ancient African beads worn by a dark-haired woman weigh her down.
explanation.walkthrough: Aggri beads are old patterned glass beads found in Ghana.
explanation.definitionFit: To trouble or distress someone is to weigh heavily upon them.

clue.text: Ye sent for the Marquess?

indicators.note: the letters of the words given are rearranged to stand for the nobleman

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether you summoned the nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: The Marquess of Steyne is the wicked nobleman in Thackeray's Vanity Fair; the anagram of YE SENT gives his name, with only a weak 'for' signalling it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Steyne, a marquess, is the villainous peer of Thackeray's novel Vanity Fair.

clue.text: Snowman

parts.note: not a figure made of snow but a man who lives in the snow

explanation.surface: A figure built from snow.
explanation.walkthrough: The one word reads as a figure of snow, but means a man of the Arctic snows; the name is now often considered offensive.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of an Arctic people, at home in the snow.

clue.text: Secret agents have a springy air!

indicators.note: a new air, or tune, for the word springy means its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Spies who walk with a bounce in their step.
explanation.walkthrough: 'air' signals the anagram: the letters of SPRINGY are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of spies working together is a network of secret agents.

clue.text: He's up the pole!

parts.note: up the pole is slang for mad, but here it means literally living on top of a pillar

explanation.surface: Someone says a man has gone mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up the pole' means crazy, but the hermit saints of early Christianity lived on top of pillars.
explanation.definitionFit: An early Christian ascetic who lived atop a pillar, like Simeon.

clue.text: There's a hush about the meeting; it's very calm

indicators.note: the call for a hush goes round, about, the word for a meeting

parts.note: sh is the sound made to call for a hush
a moot is an assembly or meeting

explanation.surface: A gathering falls silent and all is peaceful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts MOOT inside SH.
explanation.definitionFit: Calm water is flat and even, without ripples.

clue.text: The clue that makes love laugh?

definitions.text: The clue that makes love laugh?

parts.words: The clue that makes love laugh?
parts.note: the saying runs that love laughs at locksmiths, being able to open any door; a clue here is a means of opening

explanation.surface: A setter wonders what clue would amuse a lover.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'Love laughs at locksmiths' says love gets through every lock: what lets it through is the one thing that opens all doors.
explanation.definitionFit: A single device opening every lock in a building is what lets love laugh at locks.

clue.text: Dickensian school house for males

indicators.note: the letters of males are rearranged to stand for the school

explanation.surface: A boys' boarding house in a Dickens novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Salem House is David Copperfield's school, run by Mr Creakle; the anagram of MALES gives its name, with only 'for' signalling it.
explanation.definitionFit: The boys' school in Dickens's David Copperfield was called by this name, with House added.

clue.text: One who makes his points playfully and painstakingly?

definitions.text: One who makes his points playfully and painstakingly?

parts.words: One who makes his points playfully and painstakingly?
parts.note: in rugby a try scores points at play, and someone who tries hard works painstakingly

explanation.surface: A person who argues in a light-hearted yet careful manner.
explanation.walkthrough: A rugby player scoring a try makes points 'playfully'; someone who makes every effort tries 'painstakingly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who tries: a rugby scorer of tries, or a person who always makes an effort.

clue.text: It's forbidden to give thanks and make rude noises

parts.note: ta is an informal British word for thank you
to boo is to jeer rudely

explanation.surface: It is not done to thank someone and then jeer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something prohibited by custom, banned or off-limits.

clue.text: " Turn the key deftly in the wards' (Keats)

definitions.text: " Turn the key deftly in the wards' (Keats)

parts.words: " Turn the key deftly in the wards' (Keats)
parts.note: a gap-fill quotation from Keats's sonnet To Sleep, the gap describing well-greased lock wards

explanation.surface: A line from Keats with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's sonnet To Sleep has 'Turn the key deftly in the oiled wards'; wards are the ridges inside a lock.
explanation.definitionFit: Lubricated with grease, so a lock's wards turn smoothly.

clue.text: Does it help to keep up those bell-bottoms? Rummy idea!

definitions.text: Does it help to keep up those bell-bottoms? Rummy idea!

parts.words: Does it help to keep up those bell-bottoms? Rummy idea!
parts.note: sailors' bell-bottom trousers might seem to need braces, and splicing a ship's rope of that name meant a rum ration

explanation.surface: A wry question about what holds up a sailor's trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: Bell-bottoms are sailors' trousers, held up by braces; 'splice the main brace' is the naval order for an extra tot of rum, hence 'Rummy idea'.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal rope controlling a ship's main yard; splicing it is the Royal Navy phrase for issuing rum.

clue.text: Pigeons for baseball-players

definitions.meaning: racing birds trained to fly back to their loft
a home run in baseball is hit by such a player, so a batter scoring home runs

explanation.surface: Birds suited to sportsmen in America.
explanation.walkthrough: A homing pigeon is a homer; in baseball a homer is a home run, and the clue stretches it to those who hit one.
explanation.definitionFit: Racing birds that fly back to their loft; in baseball a home run, and so its hitters.

clue.text: Paolo is unusually severe on him!

indicators.note: the letters of severe on are arranged in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Someone named Paolo is being unusually harsh to a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusually' signals the anagram of SEVERE ON; Paolo is the Venetian Renaissance painter's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Paolo Caliari, called after his birthplace Verona, was a Venetian Renaissance painter.
